criteria.criterion: The change description and a doc comment on the gate in crates/athena-core/src/reading.rs name the root cause: reading validation never compared reading scope with the producer/verifier deadline; the fix sits in build_reading.
criteria.evidence: I read the diff. The doc comment on `check_reading_size` (reading.rs:185-193) says "Root cause: reading validation never compared the reading's scope with the producer and verifier deadlines … so the fix sits in `build_reading`". The CHANGELOG entry says the same thing and says the gate is called from `build_reading`.

criteria.criterion: A new unit test in athena-core builds a reading whose forecast wall_time_s.p50 exceeds budget.producer_timeout_s and asserts build_reading returns an error whose message tells the reader to pick one deliverable and name the rest as follow-up requests. Run cargo test -p athena-core.
criteria.evidence: `a_reading_forecasting_more_than_the_producer_timeout_is_refused_with_advice_to_pick_one_deliverable` passed when I ran it. It calls the real `build_reading` with p50 5000, producer timeout 3000 and verifier timeout 10000. It checks that the error contains "pick one deliverable", "follow-up request" and "producer_timeout_s of 3000s". Without the gate, `unwrap_err()` would panic on Ok, so the test fails without the change.

criteria.criterion: A companion test shows a reading with p50 within both deadlines is still accepted, and a test with p50 above only verifier_timeout_s is refused; the oversize tests fail if the gate is removed and use a generic oversize forecast, not one job's data. Run cargo test -p athena-core.
criteria.evidence: These tests passed when I ran them. `a_reading_within_both_timeouts_is_accepted` accepts p50 30 and the boundary value 2400. `a_reading_forecasting_more_than_only_the_verifier_timeout_is_refused` refuses p50 2700 with producer 3000 and verifier 2400. `a_decline_is_not_held_to_the_deadlines` accepts a decline. The forecasts come from a generic `sized_reading` helper, not from any job's data. The refusal tests call `unwrap_err()`, so they fail if the gate is removed.

criteria.criterion: The change refuses more readings and the higher refusal rate is intended: expected 3% of newly refused readings (only readings forecasting a p50 wall time beyond a configured timeout).  Existing tests and the default athena.toml readings still pass: cargo test --workspace.
criteria.evidence: Athena's recorded `cargo test --locked` passed (1591 tests). The default athena.toml timeouts are 3000 and 2400, and the existing fake readers forecast far less. Athena's replay found 0 of 50 accepted readings newly refused, which is within the declared 3% plus 5 points. The CHANGELOG says the refusal rate rises on purpose and labels 3% as an unmeasured estimate.

criteria.criterion: cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets and cargo test --workspace all pass.
criteria.evidence: Athena's records show all three checks passed on this tree.

criteria.criterion: CHANGELOG.md records the new reading size gate.
criteria.evidence: There is a new first bullet under Unreleased / Added: "A reading size gate. Root cause: …". It names the function, the config keys, the rule that a p50 equal to the limit is allowed, that declines are not gated, the retry message, and the estimated refusal rate. It is written for an outside reader.

findings.summary: The gate compares the whole job's forecast time with the time allowed for a single run, so it can refuse readings that would actually finish.
findings.evidence: `ForecastOutput.wall_time_s` is documented as "From dispatch to the final verdict, in seconds" (athena-context/src/outputs.rs:111). That covers the producer, the checks and the verifier together. The gate compares this total with the smaller of the two per-run timeouts. So a job whose producer and verifier runs each fit their own limit can still be refused, for example 1500s + 1000s = 2500s against a 2400s verifier limit. The doc comment and error text also overstate the case: "no single run can finish it" does not follow from the job-wide number. The user-accepted reading asked for exactly this comparison, and the replay found no false refusals in 50 readings, so this is not major. A tighter fix would be either a per-role forecast, or comparing p50 with the sum of the producer and verifier timeouts while keeping the per-run limit as a separate check.

findings.summary: The reader is never told the deadlines up front; it only finds out after a refusal.
findings.evidence: The refusal message goes back to the reader through `ReadError::Refused` (reading.rs:518-524), so the retry loop does work. But nothing in the reader's guidance tells it the deadlines ahead of time. The reading listed outputs.rs as an optional deliverable, so leaving it unchanged is within scope.

summary: The candidate adds `check_reading_size` and calls it from `build_reading` after the forecast is validated. It refuses a reading that names a capability when its forecast median (p50) wall time is above `budget.producer_timeout_s` or `budget.verifier_timeout_s`. The refusal tells the reader to pick one deliverable and name the rest as follow-up requests, and that message goes back to the reader once through the existing correction loop. Four new unit tests call the real `build_reading` with generic forecasts: one over the producer limit only, one over the verifier limit only, one within both limits (including p50 exactly at the limit), and one decline, which is not gated. All four passed when I ran them, and the two refusal tests fail without the gate. The doc comment and the CHANGELOG entry name the root cause and explain why the fix belongs in `build_reading`. Athena's recorded fmt, clippy and test checks pass, and the replay found no false refusals among 50 accepted readings. Only reading.rs and CHANGELOG.md changed, both on the deliverables list. One minor soundness point: the forecast covers the whole job but is compared with a single run's time limit, so the gate leans strict and can refuse readings that would finish. That is what the accepted reading asked for, so it does not fail the verdict.
